ORAL ANSWERSTO QUESTIONS 
Foreign Investment in Print Media 
*81.    SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH: † 
  DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have now settled the issue of foreign 
investment/participation in the print media; 
(b) whether it is a fact that at present foreign news agencies are only 
allowed to distribute news within the country through an Indian news agency 
owned and managed by Indians; 
(c) if so, whether his Ministry is considering a review of the existing 
policy for operation of foreign news agencies in the country; and 
(d) if so, the decisions taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OFTHE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The extent policy in force since 1956 requires that the foreign news 
agencies distribute news in this country only through the Indian news 
agencies. 
(c) and (d) It is felt necessary to consult with media persons/industry 
connected with the news agencies in order to ascertain if the 1956 policy on 
news agencies needs a detailed review given the rapid technological/ other 
changes noticed in the meantime. 
SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH: Sir, with regard to part (a), he says "Yes, Sir". 
Could the distinguished Minister kindly expand this laconic reply as to what is 
precisely being done? 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri K. Natwar 
Singh. 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir, as far as the FDI in print media is 
concerned, the Government has come with a concrete policy. It has three 
distinct components. The first is a 26 per cent cap on FDI in newsprint, with 
adequate safeguard on editorials and ed itors, and three-fourths being Indian 
directors. Then, there is the second component on publication of Indian 
edition of foreign magazines, scientific speciality and sports; and the third is 
about a 74 per cent FDI in publication of foreign magazine, speciality 
scientific. These are the three distinct components, as far as the FDI print 
policy is concerned. 
SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH: What steps have been taken to implement this 
executive decision of the Government? 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir, we have already come up with 
distinct guidelines. The guidelines are in place with all the structure 
safeguards. We, till date, have received two proposals for publication of Indian 
editions of foreign magazines which have been permitted. And five proposals 
have come. As far as FDI in the newspaper is concerned, till date, we have no 
proposals.

DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, there has been a big 
controversy for the past 40-50 years. They have broken the rule to allow the 
foreign people to invest in the print media. I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister, through you, Sir, what he has achieved till now and what are the 
advantages. In spite of the controversy, so many newspapers wanting and some 
not wanting, the Government has taken a decision. So, I would like to know 
through you, Sir, what they have achieved till today, how much money they 
have received, what is the advantage they have received and what care they 
have taken to see that the foreign media do not dominate the Indian media. 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PR ASAD: Sir, the hon. Member would very 
much like to know that we had the widest consultation possible, including the 
matter being referred to the Standing Committee. The Standing Committee 
gave its Reports. While taking a policy decision, we have sought to allay all 
the apprehensions and address all the concerns that the predominance of 
Indian sector must be there. All the adequate guidelines are there. But there was 
a great demand from the media sector itself to allow this FDI in the newspaper 
print. Five proposals are there, two have been allowed. As far as the newspaper 
part is concerned, they are not there. But I wish to assure the hon. Members 
that adequate safeguards are there to allay all the concerns which they have 
expressed in the detailed guidelines issued in this behalf. 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, my question is: What 
advantage have they got by allowing this? He must give a reply. He has not 
given a reply. What advantage has the Government got by allowing this 
controversial policy?

*82.    MISS MABEL REBELLO.† 
SHRISANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister of SHIPPING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any proposal of introducing inland water 
transport system in all cities that have some river running through it; 
(b) whether Government plans to offer inland water transport as an 
economical transport service to the people; and 
(c) if so, by when such transportation system is likely to be introduced in all 
cities that have rivers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING 
(SHRI DILIP KUMAR MANSUKHLAL GANDHI): (a) and (c) No, Sir. Do 
not arise. 
(b) Yes, Sir. Government are committed to the development of inland water 
transport as an efficient, environment friendly and economical means of transport 
for cargo and passengers. With this end in view the Ganga from Haldia to 
Allahabad, the Brahmaputra from Dhubri to Sadiya and the West Coast canal 
from Kottapuram to Kollam along with Champakara and Udyogmandal canals 
have been declared as National Waterways.

*84.     SHRIBHAGATRAM MANHAR: † 
SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that participants at the Pravasi Bharatiya Diwas 
celebrations held in January, 2003 hae expressed disappointment at the state of 
health care in India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether a large number of delegates have recommended that the state of 
health care be improved through modern and state of the art technology 
available in the world; and 
(d) if so, the steps Government propose to take on the suggestions made 
by the delegates at the above Conference? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE(SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
During the Pravasi Bharatiya Diwas Celebrations held in January, 2003, 
while acknowledging the significant improvements in Health status since 
independence, some of the participants also expressed concern and gave 
suggestions about improving the state of health care in India. Some of the 
points raised by the participants in this regard are as follows: 
(i) There is a need for improving quality in Public Health Services. 
(ii) There is a need to substantially increase the investment in the health 
sector, where NRI/PIOs can make a contribution. 
(iii) Greater focus is required on preventive and promotive initiatives. 
(iv) There is an increasing trend of life style related diseases in the country. 
(v) As the patent laws of India are not on par with the developed countries, 
the country has not been able to realize its potential for 
development/discovery of new products. 
† The question was -actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Bhagatram Mannar. 
13 

RAJYA  SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
While the Government initiative in Public Health have recorded 
noteworthy success over time leading to progressive improvement of many 
demographic/epidemiological/infrastructural indicators, there is a need for 
enhancement of Public Health investment to bring about a qualitative change 
in the Health scenario. 
To fill the gaps in the health facilities, in our Health Policy, 2002, it has 
been envisaged to increase the Health Sector expenditure to 6% of the GDP by 
the year 2010 from the current level of 5.2%. Of this 5.2%, only 0.9% is 
provided by Public Sector investment. It is envisaged to increase it to 2%. 
To meet the objectives of reducing various types of inequalities and 
imbalances between economic classes, it is envisaged to increase the sectoral 
outlay in the Primary Health Sector which would come up to 55% of the 
whole Public Health Investment. 
Quality of Public Health Services is closely linked with the quantity and 
quality of investment through public funding in the Primary Health Sector. 
With the increased investment in public health, it is planned to improve the 
quality standards. It is also envisaged to strengthen laboratory facilities and 
technical expertise so as to strengthen our food and drug administration. 
Health being a State subject, the State Government have a very important 
role to play in this regard. It is expected that the State Governments allocate 
8% of their budget to the health sector by 2010 so as to bring about an increased 
investment in this sector.

Pending cases in various courts 
†*86. SHRI GAYA SINGH: Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of cases pending in various courts of the country; and 
(b) the steps being taken for disposal of such cases? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): 
(a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Details are given in Statement I and II. (See below) 
(b) Both Government and Judiciary are concerned about the huge 
pendency of cases in courts. A series of steps have been taken by the 
Government for the speedy disposal of cases. High Courts have been 
requested to implement the recommendations of the Malimath Committee to 
streamline procedure which will, inter-alia, expedite 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
22 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
disposal of pending cases. Government have also been constantly reviewing 
the accumulation of arrears in courts. Besides reviewing and increasing judge 
strength of High Courts every three years, Government have set 
up/encouraged alternative models of dispute resolution including conciliaton, 
mediation and arbitration. Special tribunals like Central Administrative 
Tribunal, State Administrative Tribunals, Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, 
Labour Courts, Consumer Courts etc., have been set up to expedite the 
disposal of cases. Information Technology is being used in generation of 
causelists, providing information to the litigants/advocates etc., for speedy 
disposal of cases. A Pilot project has been started for Networking and 
Computerisation of City Courts in the four major metrocities of Delhi, 
Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai to serve as a model. The project is aimed at 
augmenting capacities of courts and speeding up their disposal through better 
court management with the help of information technology. 
Civil Procedure Code has been amended and the amendments have been 
brought into force with effect from 1.07.2002 which, inter-alia, limit the 
number of adjournments which can be granted to a party to three, provide for 
speedy process service by speed post, courier service, fax or e-mail, authorise 
the court to fix time limit for oral arguments and provide for a number of 
other measures aimed at ensuring expeditious disposal of cases. Permanent 
Lok Adalats are being set up for expeditious resolution of disputes relating to 
public utilities. 
Fast Track Courts have been set up to speed up the trial of delayed cases, 
and in particular the cases of undertrials who have been in jail for a long time. 
State Governments and Union Territories have been requested to fill up 
vacant posts of judges/magistrates and supporting staff in District/ 
Subordinate Courts.

*90. DR. ABRAR AHMED: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of public sector/private companies which have been 
closed in Rajasthan during the last three years as on March, 2002 and how 
many out of them have been referred to BIFR; and 
(b) the steps taken for the revival of these industries? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN 
JAITLEY): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) No public sector enterprise of the Central Government in Rajasthan 
has been closed as on March 2002, whereas, ten companies in the private 
sector have been closed from the year 1999 to March 2002. Two Central 
Public Sector Enterprises and 159 companies in the p-ivate sector have been 
referred to Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR). 
(b) The reference to BIFR, is in itself a process under which revival of 
the sick company is attempted. Under Sick Industrial Companies (Special 
Provision) Act, 1985, BIFR, wherever feasible, sanction rehabilitation 
schemes for revival of these companies by various measures under the Act 
which include restructuring of the capital, induction of fresh funds by the 
promoters, including Government for public sector companies, change of 
management, reliefs and concessions by financial institutions/ Banks, reliefs 
and concessions by the State and Central Government in the form of 
reschedulement of dues, grants etc.

redius of 7 kms. Each PHC coveres on an average 27 villages.

(b) As per the norms prescribed for establishing primary health care 
facilities in rural areas of the country, a Sub-Centre is established for every 
5000 population; a Primary Health Centre (PHC) for every 30,000 population; 
and a Community Health Centre (CHC) for every 1,20,000 population. In 
hilly, desert and tribal areas, the population norm is 3000, 20,000 and 80,000

Year Plan period. Accordingly, during the Xth Five Year Plan, it is expected that 
additionally 8208 Sub-centres, 1714 PHCs and 2562 CHCs will be established 
which will enable reaching the norm as per 1991 population.

Patenting of Vastu, Vedas etc. by Germany 
†*94.      SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRI MOTILALVORA: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Vastu, Vedas, Ayurveda and Gayatri 
Mantras have been patented in Germany; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
58 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(c) whether some other Indian items are also being patented in some other 
countries in the similar way; 
(d) if so, the reaction of Government thereto; and 
(e) the action taken by Government for its annulment? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN 
JAITLEY): (a) to (e) The reported patenting of Vastu, Vedas, Ayurveda and 
Gayatri Mantras in Germany is factually not correct. Further, Vastu, Vedas, 
Ayurveda and Gayatri Mantras are Prima-facie not patentable under patent 
laws. Patents are only granted to a process or a product which meets the 
criteria of patentability, namely, novelty, inventiveness and industrial 
applicability.The issue needs to be distinguished from the usage of such words 
for trade promotion for which trade marks registration is sought/obtained under 
appropriate laws by commercial and other organisations. Such usage is not 
expressly inadmissible under the trademarks laws of various countries, 
including India. 
Intellectual property rights, including patents, are granted under the 
sovereign prerogative of countries according to their respective laws and have 
territorial effect only, that is they are effective only in the country of grant. 
As and when information is received about patents being obtained on 
certain items which are not considered patentable and which affect Indian 
interests, steps are taken to assess whether the grant of such patent can be 
challenged under the patent laws of the country concerned. 
Earlier a patent granted in the United States of America on the use of 
turmeric in wound healing was successfully challenged and was also 
cancelled by the Patent Office of the country concerned. Similarly, a patent 
on the fungicidal property of neem, granted in Europe, was successfully 
challenged. The claims of the patent on Basmati Ricelines and grains granted in 
the United States of America which had the potential of affecting India's 
commercial interest were also challenged. The said claims were subsequently 
cancelled by the United States Patent and Trademark Office and the title of 
the patent was also amended. 
Intellectual property rights, including patents, are essentially private rights 
and are normally challenged by the person(s) whose interests are 
affected/jeopardised.

slowdown in November 2002, when a growth of 3-6% was registered. CMIE, 
however, has revised upwards their forecast of growth in the Index of Industrial

September 2001 -02. While some consumer durables have done well, in IIP,

decline of (-) 7.1% in the production index of food products. Other main points 
highlighted in the CMIE report are as below: 
• The poor monsoon of the current year severely affected oilseeds 
production. 
• The core sector also slowed down in November 2002. 
• Steel, cement, ready-made garments, automobiles and select 
category of consumer durables have fared extremely well. The 
government's initiatives in consumer durables have fared 
extremely well. The government's initiatives in setting up road 
projects across the country have boosted demand for cement and

operating efficiency but mostly due to saving in interest costs.

scale sector and exports in its credit policy for 2002-03. It also 
aims at facilitating better credit delivery and moving forward

implicating cigarette smoking as a cause of coronary artery disease, stroke, 
obstructive lung disease, peripheral vascular disease, pregnancy complications

cancers of oral cavity, larynx, oesophagus, urinary bladder, kidney, stomach, 
pancreas, cervix and haematopoietic system. Recent studies have also

Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation ofTrade and 
Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Bill, 2001, which-has been 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 7th March, 2001, inter-alia, contains 
provisions for prohibiting advertisement of all tobacco products.

Trade treaty with SAARC countries 
472. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India has signed a trade treaty with SAARC members; 
(b) if so, the highlights of the treaty; 
(c) whether multi-national operating in these SAAC countries are likely to 
take undue advantages of concessional duty facility to flood Indian market 
with their goods especially food items; and 
(d) in what manner Government propose to tackle this problem? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY): (a) and (b)The Agreement 
establishing the SAARC Preferential Trading Arrangement (SAPTA) was signed 
on 11 th April, 1993 in Dhaka by all seven SAARC countries namely, India, 
Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and the Maldives. SAFTA 
provides a framework for the exchange of tariff concessions with a view to 
promoting trade and economic cooperation among the SAARC member 
countries. 
(c) and (d) The multi-national operating in these SAARC countries are 
unlikely to take undue advantage of concessional duty facility to flood the 
Indian market with their goods since tariff preferences are subject to Rules of 
Origin under the SAPTA Agreement. To qualify for preferential treatment under 
SAPTA, goods must fulfill the following Rules of Origin prescribed in the 
Agreement:— 
(i) For developing Member countries of SAARC, value addition/ local 
content in the exporting country should be 40%. 
(ii) In case a product is processed in more than one member country of 
SAARC, the cumulative value addition/local content requirement 
is 50%. 
(iii) There is a relaxation of 10 per cent in these criteria for the least 
developed SAARC countries, namely, Bangladesh, Bhutan, 
Maldives and Nepal.

495. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have decided to apeal in the World 
Trade Organisation Appellate Body against the Compliance Panel Report on 
cotton bed linen, which favoured the imposition of anti-dumping duty on the 
product; and 
(b) if so, the latest position of the case? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY): (a) and (b) Indian had 
resorted to World Trade Organiza tion's (WTO) Dispute Settlement 
Mechanism and challenged the anti dumping duty imposed by European 
Communities (EC) on imports of bed linen from India. On 12 March 2001 the 
Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) adopted the Appellate Body Report and the 
Panel Report as modified by the Appellate Body, in this dispute. These Reports 
concluded that the EC's imposition of definitive antidumping duties on 
imports of cotton-type bed linen from India had been inconsistent with the 
Anti-dumping Agreement. Pursuant to the recommendations of these Reports, 
the DSB requested the European Communities to bring its measure into 
conformity with its obligatinos under the Anti-dumping Agreement. 
Subsequently EC undertook a review of the anti-dumping measure and re-
determined the level of anti-dumping duty. However, the application of the duty 
was suspended. India strongly disagreed with the re-determination and at its 
request a Compliance Panel had been constituted to examine the consistency of 
measures taken by EC in compliance with the decision of the DSB in the 
original bed linen dispute with EC. The Compliance Panel has concluded that 
EC has implemented the recommendations of the DSB in the original bed 
linen dispute. 
India has appealed to the WT O's Appellate Body certain issues of law 
and legal interpretations covered in the Compliance Panel Report in this dispute. 
A Notice of Appeal was filed by India before the Dispute Settlement Body of 
the WTO on 8th January, 2003, after which the appellate proceedings have 
commenced.

AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY): (a) and (b) An informal 
meeting of about 20Trade Ministers of Member States of WTO was held 
inTokyo at the invitation of Japanese Government from 14-16 February 2003. 
The Indian delegation was jointly led by Minister of Commerce & Industry and 
Law & Justice and Minister of Agiculture. The Director General of WTO also 
attended the informal mini-Ministerial meeting. 
This meeting reviewed all major WTO issues under negotiations in the 
on-going Doha Work Programme, including market access for agricultural and 
non-agricultural products and services;TRIPS and Public Health; Special and 
DifferentialTreatment; Implementation-related issues and concerns; Rules; and 
the Singapore issues of Trade and Investment. Trade and Competition Policy, 
Transparency in Government Procurement and Trade Facilitation. 
At this meeting, India forcefully articulated the need to restore the 
development agenda as the central focus of WTO negotiations, as mandated 
in the Doha Ministerial Declaration. India strongiy expressed its concern over 
the slow progress in the area of development-related issues such as TRIPS 
and Public Health; implementation issues and special and differential 
treatment issues and stated that the success or otherwise of the forthcoming 
Cancum Ministerial Conference of the WTO 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
irvSeptember this year would greatly depend on the resolution of these issues. 
Participants from many other developing countries such as Barazil, Kenya, 
Costa Rica, Nigeria, Lesotho and Senegal strongly supported India's 
statement. 
Since agriculture was a priority sector for all countries, India pointed out 
that satisfactory resolution with respect to distortions in global agricultural 
trade can take place only if both domestic support and export subsidies were 
substantially reduced or eliminiated in the developed countries. India strongly 
emphasized the highest priority that it would give to the protection of its 
farmers and their well being. India also stressed the need for sufficient special 
and differential treatment provisions for developing countries, such as the use of 
special safeguard measures to prevent surge in imports. It pointed out the lack of 
flexibility it had on market access in agriculture. 
In respect of non-agricultural products, India strongly advocated 
increased market access for products of export interest to India such as textiles, 
leather goods. Expressing strong interest in the services' negotiations, India 
asked for greater liberalization in the movement of natural persons. 
On Singapore issues, India reiterated its stand that these issues did not fall 
within the purview of WTO which should focus on trade related issues only. 
In the area of Rules, India called for stronger disciplines in anti-dumping and 
anti-subsidy so as to ensure that the market access achieved through reduction 
in tariffs and elimination of non-tariff barriers is not negated through trade 
defence measures. 
Since this was an informal meeting, discussions were in the form of 
exchange of views of participating countries with no declared outcome. The 
object was to see how further progress can be made in taking forward the Doha 
Work Programme by the time of the Fifth Ministerial Conference to be held in 
Cancum, Mexico this year. The Ministers in this meeting resolved to make a 
fresh effort to achieve progress in areas, which are of vital interest to the 
developing countries. 
(c) Continuous dialogues with stake holders have been held to finalise India's 
position on various WTO issues. Based on these inputs, India seeks to protect 
its national interests by actively participating in the 
98 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
negotiations and articulating its position effectively. Further, it is also making 
bilateral, plurilateral and multilateral efforts, both with developed and 
developing country members, so as to ensure that interests of developing 
countries, including India are fully protected. India would make utmost efforts to 
ensure a balanced outcome at the end of the negotiations that would try to protect 
the interests of all WTO Members and also to ensure that the development-
oriented focus of the Doha mandate is fully preserved in the final results of the 
negotiations.

Adulteration in bottled water 
503. SHRIDATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that bottled water available in various 
markets in Delhi and other places contains harmful pesticides; 
(b) if so, whether the Department of Prevention of Food Adulteration has 
totally failed to check such adulteration in bottled water; 
(c) whether Government have fixed any responsibility on PFA 
department about the adulteration; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) Packaged Drinking Water 
106 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
has been declared as an item of food under PFA Act, 1954 vide notification GSR 
No. 202 (E) dated 21.3.2001. Prior to that packaged Drinking Water was not an 
item of food and hence was not covered under PFA Act, 1954. 
The standards for Packaged Drinking Water and Mineral Water have been 
prescribed under PFA Rules, 1955 inline with the standards prescribed by 
Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS).These products are under compulsory 
Certification Scheme of BIS. 
As per the standards, Presticide Residue should be "below detectable limits" 
when tested in accordance with relevant methods as prescribed by BIS. 
The samples of Packaged Drinking Water and Mineral Water analyzed as per 
BIS method were conforming to the prescribed level of Presticide Residue. 
However, in an independent study by Centre for Science Environment, New 
Delhi, samples of Packaged Drinking Water and Mineral Water were stated to 
contain Pesticide Residue because of difference in the test method adopted by 
CSF. 
The standards of Packaged Drinking Water and Mineral water have been 
reviewed on the advise of BIS and a draft notification has been published 
vide GSR No. 111(E) dated 18.2.2003 proposing following amendments: 
(i) Pesticide residues considered individually - 0.0001 mg/litre. 
(The analysis shall be conducted by using Internationally established test 
methods meeting the residue limits specified herein above). 
(ii)Total Pesticide residues - 0.0005 mg/litre. 
(The analysis shall be conducted by using Internationally established test 
methods meeting the residue limits specified herein above)." 
It is informed by the Government of NCT of Delhi that they have 
analysed 117 samples of Packaged Drinking Water and Mineral Water. In all the 
samples, Pesticide Residue were not detected by the method of analysis 
prescribed by BIS.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND

to the notice of the government. These cases have been investigated. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

RAJYA  SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) is highly effective vaccine but as with every other 
medication, a small number of children (5-10%) don't respond to the vaccine. 
If the polio virus is in circulation in the areas it is likely that such children, 
who have not responded to the OPV, are likely to get afflicted with polio.The 
only way to assure 100% protection from polio is to eliminate the polio virus 
and thus stop it from circulating from child to child. It is therefore, even more 
important that every child under 5 years of age receives polio drops on every 
pulse polio day, in addition to their routine immunizations. 
The National goal is to eradicate polio from the country and obtain 
international polio-free certification by 2005. The annual strategies for 
achieving this goal are formulated and implemented on the basis of advice of a 
group of national and international experts.Two National immunization Days are 
observed throughout the country for giving polio drops to the children below 
5 years of age. In addition, sub-National Immunization days are also observed 
in States where cases are reported to be increasing. Mop-up vaccination rounds 
are also conducted in the districts and adjoining areas where new cases are 
detected. 
Following special measures have been taken with special reference to the 
States where large number of polio cases have been detected:- 
(i) In order to improve the detection and vaccination of missed children, 
the house-to-house vaccination teams have been strengthened with 
the addition of third member preferably a women from local 
community. 
(ii) House-to-house vaccination of missed children is being done for five 
days after the booth day as against two days in other parts of the 
country. 
(iii)    Additional IEC activities are being conducted. 
(iv) The implementation of the programme is being closely monitored at the 
apex political and official levels in the Government of India as also 
in the States.

advocacy and ensuring greater participation of the people in the 
programme.

of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:

banned are still being produced, stocked and freely administered to the patients 
in the country; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard; 
(c) whether it is recognized world over that these drugs have serious side 
effects when taken for a long time and without medical advice; and

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) It is not a fact that large 
number of drugs banned globally are freely marketed in the country.There is no

ethnic groups in a given population to the drug, the availability of safer 
substitutes as well as the cost factor involved in the treatment of the diseases.

news letters etc. 75 drugs/drug formulations have so far been prohibited through 
the review process.

representatives from the medical profession, the state drug enforcement

Increase in AIDS cases 
545. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite the country spending around $40 million 
on its AIDS Control Programme, the incidence of this disease are still on the 
increase and is likely to grow from 4 million cases to 8.9 million by the 
middle of this decade; and 
(b) if so, the steps Government have taken to prevent the spread of this 
disease in the country and to bring awareness among the people to check the 
disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) In order to track the 
trends in the spread of HIV infections in the country, the National AIDS 
Control Organisation conducts a nation-wide sentinel surveillance round each 
year. This data is also used towards estimation of total HIV infections in the 
country, taking into consideration certain assumptions finalized after 
consultation with the national and international experts. The National AIDS 
Control Organisation has not made any future projection in respect of the 
number of HIV infections. 
Accordingly, the numbers of persons infected with HIV were 3.5 million in 
1998; 3.7 million in 1999; 3.86 million in 2000 and 3.97 million in 2001. These 
estimates indicate that there has not been any unsurge in the spread of HIV 
infection in the country. However, this number is a cause of concern and there 
can be no slackening of efforts to prevent and control the spread of this 
disease. 
In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, Govt, of 
India has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control Programme, currently 
under implementation throughout the country as a centrally sponsored 
scheme with the following components:— 
Preventive interventions for high risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer counseling and 
behaviour change communications. 
Preventive interventions for the general population through programmes 
for blood safety, voluntary counseling and testing services, 
153 

RAJYA  SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
information education and communication(IEC) and awareness building among 
adolescents and sensitization for the AIDS Vaccine Initative. 
Provision of low cost care and support services by providing community 
care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and prevention of 
occupational exposure. 
Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including interventions and public-private partnerships. 
Build technical and managerial capacities for programme implementation 
through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring and Evaluation, Technical resource 
groups, operational research and Programme Management. 
In order to increase awareness among the general population in order to 
motivate behaviour change, the State AIDS Control Societies are 
implementing various IEC activities under the programme. National AIDS 
Control Organisation is utilizing the services of the different units of the 
Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and Prasar Bharati 
(DOORDARSHAN & AAKASHVANI) for dissemination of messages. 
Services of Directorate of Advertising and Visual Publicity. Song and Drama 
Division and Press Information Bureau are being used for outreach activities using 
print, electronic and outdoor media, in various parts of the country. 
For sensitization of children and young people, School AIDS Education 
Programme, the UniversitiesTalk AIDS and VillageTalk AIDS Programmes are 
being implemented in collaboration with Ministry ofYouth Affairs and Sports. 
The programme has an inbuilt monitoring and evaluation component, which 
tracks the implementation of various components of the programme and also 
ensures evidence based programming.

Under the provisions of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995,

centralized database of the total number of registered cable operators and

the pay channels. Under the provisions of the Cable Television Networks 
(Regulation) Amendment Act 2002, the Central Government may specify the 
maximum amount which a cable operator may demand from the subscribers

channels). However, there is no provisions to regulate the charges for pay 
channels, which would

THE MINISTER OF STATE INTHE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (DR. SANJAY PASWAN): (a) Yes, Sir. The 
Department of Women and Child Development is implementing various 
schemes for women welfare. Of these, two schemes which have been recently 
launched are:- 
(i) In 2000-01, Swayamsidha, an Integrated Scheme for holistic 
empowerment of women was launched.

(b) and (c) Government of India is implementing the National Scheme of 
Liberation and Rehabilitation of Scavengers and their Dependents (NSLRS) 
since 1992.The objective of NSLRS is to liberate the scavengers from their 
existing hereditary obnoxious and inhuman occupation of manually removing 
of night soil and filth and to provide for and engage them in alternative and 
dignified occupations. The main components of the scheme are time bond 
survey for identification of scavengers, training and rehabilitation.The full cost of 
training is borne by the Government of India, towards rehabilitation of 
scavengers, projects costing upto Rs. 50,000/- for each beneficiary are 
financed by way of a prescribed financial package comprising of 50% 
subsidy subject to a ceiling of Rs. 10,000/- per project, 15% of project cost as 
Margin Money Loan (MML) which is shared between the Central 
Government and State Governments in the ratio 49:51 and the balance amount 
is provided as loan at concessional rate of interest by the National Safai 
Karamacharis Finance and Development Corporation (NSKFDC). In order to 
accelerate and energise the pace of NSLRS, the concept of Sanitary Mart has 
been introduced in the year 1999-2000 for rehabilitation of scavengers in groups. 
Besides this, a Central legislation namely, "The Employment of Manual 
Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993" has 
been enacted to convert the existing dry latrines and construction of pour flush 
latrines. Housing and Urban Development Corporation (HUDCO) under the 
Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation has taken up

MOTION OF THANKS ON PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS -- Contd. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Discussion on the Motion of Thanks on 
the President's Address.   Shri J. Chitharanjan. 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN (Kerala): Madam Deputy Chairperson, I 
am grateful to you for allowing me to participate in this discussion. 
First of all, I would like to pay my homage to Late Kalpana Chawla 
and six other astronauts, who died in the recent accident in the disintegration 
of space shuttle, Columbia. 
Madam, then, I deal with the Iraq situation, in the President's 
Address. All of us know that, at present, the Iraq issue is of utmost concern for 
the entire international community and of course, for the Indian people also. 
Unfortunately, the Government of India has not made its policy clear in this 
respect. Paragraph 71 of the President's Address says, "We share the concern 
of the entire world on the unhappy situation relating to Iraq. We have deep 
interest in peace, stability and security in that region. We hope that the wisdom 
of the international community, expressed through the UN Security Council, will 
result in a peaceful resolution of this matter..." Yesterday, the hon. Prime 
Minister has made a speech at the business forum of the NAM. There also he 
did not spell out as to what exactly is the policy of India in this respect is. The 
sole Super Power, the United States, declares some of the States as rogue 
States or evil States. They say that 'the countries, which have large amount of 
arms, would be attacked1. They say that they would dictate terms to the United 
Nations Organisation itself. 
238 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
The Security Council is being asked to take a decision in their favour. And 
then they go on to say that even if the Security Council does not agree to their 
demand, they, along with their allies, would attack Iraq, and in that case U.N.'s 
existence will be in danger. This is what the American President, Mr. George 
Bush, is saying. Madam, if this thing is allowed to happen, what will be the 
outcome? America may attack Iraq tomorrow and the next day, Iran may be 
attacked and then, they may attack North Korea also, and then, some other 
country might be attacked. It might become the rule of the day; an unwritten 
rule of the day. The question is: Will we be spared? On the same ground, one 
day, India can also be attacked. In para 70, the President has stated this and I 
quote: "The Gulf region is of great importance to India. The region is a major 
source of India's energy needs, a major economic partner in trade and 
investment. Over 3.5 million Indians are engaged in the economic 
development of the Gulf countries." So, if this attack does take place, what 
would happen? The geo-political situation in the whole region will have to be 
redrafted. It will have its own repercussions and it will very much affect us. Of 
course, we have trade relations with them. We are dependent, to a large 
extent, on them for our energy requirements. Around 3.5 million Indians are 
working in the Gulf countries. If war were to break out, it will be very difficult for 
these people to remain there. I don't know whether they would be able to 
leave during war-time. For the present, this can be kept aside. But we will 
have to face the problem of rehabilitating these 3.5 million people. Will it be a 
small problem? No; it will be a very serious problem. Therefore, I want to say 
that the Government has to, categorically, declare the policy that is being 
adopted in this particular matter. I think, the Government should, categorically, 
say that we don't agree with the tactics followed by the super-powers; we don't 
agree that they have got the right to attack any country they like. No country 
should be allowed to do that. The United States is dictating terms to the United 
Nations. We should, categorically, say that we don't agree with that also. We 
should demand that some more time should be given to Iraq. Those who are 
inspecting the arms in Iraq, should be given some more time to do the testing. 
After all these tests, let the U.N. decide whether Iraq should be attacked or 
not. No individual country can take a decision over that. The Government of 
India should make this point clear. But after observing the stand taken by the 
Government, and the reluctance and hesitation on their part to categorically 
declare their policy, I am led to believe that this Government is doing so with a 
deliberate intention of wooing the United States of America.   In that 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
case, the prestige of our country will go down.   This is what I have, to say 
about that. 
Now, I come to my next point. The President has, in his speech, 
pointed out that our economy is growing at a faster pace. He has mentioned 
that problems are being solved, and that the percentage of poor people has 
come down, etc. Unfortunately, I don't agree with the views expressed by him. 
What exactly is the real situation? For example, take the case of agriculturists. 
About 65 per cent c r me people in our country depend on agriculture. The 
agricultural labour, fa rmers, etc. depend on agriculture only. For the last 3-4 
years, because of the heavy .all in production of the agricultural products, their 
life has become miserable. They have suffered severe losses. And, not only 
this, they are heavily indebted. Therefore, out of desperation, some of them 
have committed suicides.   So, this is the real situation. 
Now, I come to the question of workers. Of course, it has been 
claimed in the President's Address that the Government is committed to 
safeguard their interests. But, now, what is happening? In the public sector 
units, workers are being sent out on VRS. About eight lakh people have 
already been sent out on VRS. And, now, in all the public sector undertakings, 
the second round of sending on VRS has already started. The State Bank of 
India has decided that 60 per cent of its employees --that means more than 
1,20,000 employees -- will be sent out on VRS. If this goes on, what will be the 
situation? Of course, they will get some money at that time, but there is no 
safety. No arrangement is being made to provide them protection, in the form 
of providing alternate employment opportunities, etc. Nothing of that sort is 
being done. It will create problems. The same thing is happening in the private 
sector also. Our traditional industries, for example, beedi, weaving, cashew, 
coir and a large number of other industries are all in crises. There is no work. 
Workers are not getting proper wages. On the other hand, the Government is 
trying to amend the labour laws in a retrograde manner. Under the 
circumstances, workers are very much worried. That is why, a large number of 
Central Trade Unions like AITUC, CITU, HMS, and UTUC have joined together 
and decided at a Convention held in Delhi, on 15 th of last July to carry on a 
march to Parliament on 26 th of this month itself. But, unfortunately, the 
situation is such that it will be very difficult for us to convene ttie« march. The 
police are not allowing us.    I, alongwith Shri Gaya Singh, met hon. 
240 

[24 February. 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Home Minister. We talked to him. He was very cooperative. He talked to the 
Governor, and the Governor talked to the police officers. The police officers 
said that we would not be allowed to get out of the Ram Lila maidan. And, 
now, they are saying that we may be allowed to go a little ahead, but, 
thereafter, we will be stopped. In a democratic country like ours, why can't the 
people be allowed to carry on marches and demonstrations in streets to 
express their grievances, to raise their demands, etc? 
In the case of Iraq, in all the capitals of various countries in the world, 
big demonstrations took place. In London, it was reported that 20 lakh people 
participated in the demonstrations, but nothing happened there. They 
expressed their views against war and for peace. They raised slogans and 
conducted demonstrations. Why, in a country like ours, people are not allowed 
to conduct demonstrations and to carry on march. Therefore, I think, the 
Government should reconsider this issue. 
Thirdly, I would like to say that the President's Address, has raised 
some hopes that the Tenth Five Year Plan, which has already been approved 
by the Government, as well as, the National Development Council, is going to 
be implemented. Of course, the target set, that is, eight per cent growth is 
very high. It has been stated that about five crore jobs would be created. All 
these are laudable objectives, but, Sir, I am doubtful whether these targets 
would be achieved. Madam, for implementing the Plan, what is first required is 
resources, the financial resources. The first suggestion that is made in this 
regard is to raise 10 billion every year. That is the proposal. Madam, from 
1991 onwards since we begun to implement the globalisation or liberalisation 
programme, we have been trying to get more and more Foreign Direct 
•Investment. For the first nine years, what we have got is only $ 27 billion. 
That means, on an average, we are getting only $ 3 billion every year. During 
the last two years, I think, perhaps, it might have gone up to $ 4 billion, and, 
this year, we are getting round about $ 4 billion only. So, will it be possible, in 
the coming years, to have a sudden jump from $ 3-4 billion to $ 10 billion? 
This is one thing. 
The second thing is, another source on which we can depend on is 
the revenue resources. In the President's Address also, it has been said, "In 
the case of realisation of tax revenues, we are lagging behind." On most 
occasions, in several cases, we could not even fulfil the budgeted 
241 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February, 2003] 
targets, and the realisation was less. Therefore, the President has stated in his 
statement that two things will have to be done in this regard. The first thing that 
he has said was that realisation of tax will have to be increased, and the other 
thing which he has pointed out was that the governance should improve. 
Madam, let me say that it is always being said that workers are the main 
hindrance in the production and the working of the industry; it has been said 
that workers are preventing the flow of the FDI into the country. But, Madam, 
what will happen to these FDIs? All of them say that they want to come 
forward and express their readiness to invest money here, and pursue it for 
three or four years, but they do not get the necessary clearance from various 
Government Departments. The things do not move forward. Therefore, most of 
the people may leave. After waiting for two or three years or even four or five 
years, they will leave. Why is it so happening? It is because of the red-tapism, 
and also because of the long-binding procedures. These are basically the 
main stumbling blocks. Why couldn't this problem solved so far? How can we 
expect that it would be solved within the next one or two years? I do not think it 
can be solved within that time. 
Madam, the third thing is with regard to the tax. Even in a country like 
India, the number of people who are having -- according to the tax figures -- an 
annual income of Rs. 10 lakhs and above is only 54,000. This is the position in 
a country which is having a population of more than one billion. Madam, about 
15-20 per cent people is expected to be in a better-off position, i.e., their 
economic position has improved. If it is so, wny has the number of tax-payers 
remained so low? Madam, what happens is, only the Government employees 
or the teachers or the employees in the private sector are taxed. They will all 
be taxed because their salaries are fixed, and, from them, the tax could be 
realised at source. Therefore, it is being realised. But most of the people who 
are able to give tax, are out of the tax net. That is one thing. The other thing is, 
even if some taxes are levied on these people, most of them evade paying tax, 
and become defaulters. That is what is happening. That also is not being 
looked into seriously. Therefore, it is the question of resources. Another 
question that is to be considered in the case of resources is that of small 
savings or the national savings. In our case, the percentage of national 
savings is coming down from 25-26 per cent to 22-23 per cent. That is what 
has nappened. The steps that have been taken by the Government to re-fix 
the interest rates and to reduce the interest  rates have already proved to be a 
sort of 
242 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
disincentive to the depositors. Therefore, the possibility of increasing the 
national savings is also becoming difficult. Moreover, there are reports that the 
Government is intending to persuade the small investors to approach the 
stock exchanges, and in that case the national savings will not be raised. 
Therefore, resources do not have any prospects also. In such a situation, 
because of the difficulty in raising resources, the targets could not be attained. 
With regard to the growth rate, the first year of the Plan is going to end by 31 * 
March. But what will be the growth rate? In the Budget, it was estimated 6.5 
per cent. Later on, it was assessed 5 per cent to 5.5 per cent. Now, it has 
been assessed that it would be 4.4 per cent. Thus, we could attain only that 
much growth rate. If you look at the previous years also, we could not attain 8 
per cent growth rate during the last ten years. In some years, we have 
reached around, above 5 per cent or, at the most, 5.5 per cent. Therefore, it 
will be difficult, or, I think, it will be impossible to attain these targets, and if 
targets are not being attained, the other expectations also will be belied. 
Therefore, my suggestion is that the Government should seriously consider as 
to how the Plan could be implemented and as to how the resources could be 
realised. 
Thirdly, I would like to say in respect of communalism. The President 
has stated that Gujarat election has strengthened the democracy. He has also 
stated that we should see that communal disturbances or riots do not take 
place in any part of the country. What is happening in our country? Of course, 
in Gujarat the BJP had won the election; they had come to power. I do admit. 
But, at the same time, everyday the leaders of the VHP are proclaiming from 
the housetops that they will repeat what was done in Gujarat. What was the 
peculiar nature of developments in Gujarat? In Gujarat, peopie were 
communally divided. In fact, the people belonging to the minority communities 
were being persecuted. But, it is a fact that people belonging to the minority 
communities in Gujarat are very much afraid of their future. They are also 
complaining that when other developments took place in Gujarat, even when 
certain relief measures were announced, certain compensations were 
announced, most of the people who deserve relief and compensation were 
not given those benefits. That complaint is also there. Now, the VHP leaders 
are saying that this countrv will have to be made a Hindu Rashtra. It is very 
difficult to believe that these things are being said by these people without the 
knowledge and consent of those who are in power, or else, nobody will dare 
to do that. Every day they are coming and saying, this country -- a secular, 
democratic 
243 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February, 2003] 
country according to the Constitution -- will be made a Hindu Rashtra. Then, 
they again say that in Ayodhya the temple will be constructed. That problem is 
there. But they are adding to the problems. Take, for example, what is 
happening at Dhar near Indore in Madhya Pradesh. A problem was also 
created there. Then in Chikmagalur, another problem was created. Recently 
some of them have said that 3,000 mosques will have to be returned. Then 
somebody said that 30,000 mosques will have to be given. When all these 
things are being freely propagated from the housetops, the Government keeps 
mum on these matters. No POTA is applied against them; no law works 
against them. That is what is happening. Therefore, if the Government is 
serious to see that secularism is maintained, communal disturbances are not 
taken place and communal harmony is maintained, the Government will have to 
take serious steps with sincerity, or else, it won't help us. Now, I come to the 
other question. Madam, it has been stated in the President's Address that, it is 
the prime concern of the Government to safeguard the interests of the weaker 
sections and the working class, and to ensure welfare measures for them. But, 
what is happening? There are several labour laws in the country, and I can say 
this with confidence, that in larger parts of the country, none of the provisions 
of the labour laws is being implemented, and I am prepared to prove this fact. 
In several places, the Labour Department is quite ineffective, it is dormant, and 
that is the situation. The existing labour laws are not being implemented. That 
is one thing. Secondly, there was the Provident Fund Scheme. Under this 
scheme, a higher rate of interest used to be given on the amounts that were 
being accumulated, and finally, the workers used to get the benefit of it. But 
now, they are reducing the rate of interest on such accumulation in stages, in 
phases. Again, they are thinking of reducing the rate of interest. If this is the 
situation, how can they say that they are looking after the welfare of the 
workers? How are they favouring the workers? Madam, in the beginning, I 
have said that workers are being thrown out of employment on the basis of the 
VRS or they are being retrenched on one pretext or the other. In a country like 
ours, the biggest source of employment is the cottage and village industries, 
and not the modern industries. Of course, modern industries are also 
necessary. But, at the same time, compared to the modem industries, more 
employment would be provided by the traditional industries and the cottage 
industries. That is the situation. What is the condition of these industries? They 
are being neglected completely. Their problems are not being attended to, and 
whatever concessions used to be given in the past for the cottage, handloom 
and weaving sectors, they are 
244 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
being withdrawn one after another. Therefore, they are all in great difficulty. 
Therefore, that claim has also been negated. 
Regarding education, in the President's Address, it has been claimed 
tl *t in the matter of compulsory elementary education for children between the 
age of 6 to 14 years, all of them will be provided free education. But, what was 
the result? Last year, the amount allotted for that pioose was only half of what 
was required, and now, reports are regularly appearing in the Press, that this 
year also, that is, during 2003-04, the Budget allotment for this purpose is 
going to be very meagre, and this task will remain unfulfilled. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Mr. Chitharanjan, will you conclude now? 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: So far as the question of higher education 
and technical education is concerned, what is happening here? Now, the 
engineering colleges and the medical colleges are being given to self-
sustained institutions. What are they doing? If a student wants an admission in 
those institutions, in that case, in some institutions, you have to give Rs. 35 
lakhs. Leave aside the high fees that he has to pay, a capitation fee up to Rs. 
35 lakhs is being charged for these courses! Even for certain courses, which 
are not so important, Rs. 12 lakhs to Rs. 14 lakhs are being charged. Even for 
a B.Ed course, lakhs of rupees will have to be provided. Therefore, if these 
things go on, people belonging to the poorer sections, the lower middle class, 
and even the Government employees, including the higher ups, won't be able 
to get their wards admitted in the aforesaid courses in these institutions. How 
much salary does the highest Government officer get? I think, it is somewhere 
between Rs. 30,000/- and Rs. 40,000 per month. How can that officer make up 
Rs. 25 lakhs or Rs. 35 lakhs for the admission of just one of his children in the 
medical or engineering college? How can he raise that money? Here, we all 
say that there shall be no corruption, but these people are willing to be 
involved in that corruption. Therefore, if this continues, a situation will arise 
when the people belonging to the lower strata of the community and even the 
middle class will be denied the opportunity of getting higher education in the 
technical field, whether it be in the medical or engineering cadre. This is the 
situation. Now, in such a situation, my suggestion is that the Government will 
have to seriously consider the points raised by me, as also by some 
245 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February, 2003] 
other hon. Members in the House. Unless this is done, all the expectations of 
leading the country to a higher trajectory of growth and improving the living 
conditions of the people will become difficult to achieve. Instead of that, the 
people of this country will be thrown to misery. With these words, I conclude.

SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH : Thank you, Madam, for giving me an 
opportunity to speak on the Motion of Thanks to the President's Address 
moved by Dr. L.M. Singhvi. Madam, exactly, an year ago, while participating in

economic situation in the country and the lack of proper debate and 
discussion on such vital issues as economics that directly affect the quality of 
life of one billion people of our country. It is very unfortunate that even after 50 
years of Independence, we still have not come to realise as to what our 
priorities are. Unfortunately, we seem to be getting overwhelmed, at regular 
intervals, by many historical aberrations for which generally there are no easy 
solutions. 
Madam, I want to emphasise that we cannot turn the clock back. We 
cannot correct every mistake that had occurred some 500 or 600 years back. 
We are now living in a more civilized world, in the sense-that there are many 
checks and balances that seek to prevent flash points. We are all witnessing 
how the countries like Germany, France are able to stand-up to the aggressive 
posturing of a unipolar country like the United States, vis-avis Iraq. The world 
has become a very small global village. Thanks to the technological 
developments that have taken place in the country, the distance across the 
globe has really shrunk. The world is very different now than what it was 
earlier during the last 5,000 years. In a sense, it will not be possible any more 
for the mightier nations to subjugate the weaker nations and occupy the weak. 
We used to call the historical leaders like Alexander and Napoleon as the 
greats. But they are no longer the greats. In true interpretation of the term, 
they can be described as land-grabbers. The true leaders who have inspired 
us and whose lives have inspired us are Mahatma Gandhi, Baba Amte and 
Mother Teresa. They deserve to be called the greats, not the land-grabbers 
like Alexander because the great people, disregarding their personal interests, 
have tried to reach out to those underprivileged who have been suffering, 
regardless of the religion and caste of the person. Every religion - although it 
came into existence by promising greater peace and prosperity, order and 
tranquillity - the world history shows, unfortunately, was the source of the 
greatest sorrow and suffering. Many battles were fought in the name of 
religion. We have heard about the Crusades which were fought for 300 years. 
They have been fought in the name of religion, sectarianism, bigotism and 
fanaticism. We are seeing today the problems between various sects of 
Christianity, Islam and Hinduism.  Still, we can authoritatively say that the 
problems have

need to look into these aspects. Otherwise, we will end up nowhere, although 
there exists considerable scope for India to emerge as one of the  biggest 
outsourcing base for  manufacturers. 
Sir, I agree that as a fallout of economic reforms, the Government 
should, as far as possible, disengage itself from business. This does not 
automatically mean that the Government has no role to play in the economic 
development of this country. The primary point to be kept in mind is - it is one 
of the points which has been made clear - that privatisation should not lead to 
creation of monopolies in this country. Even the hardcore protagonists of 
privatisation say that monopolies in the private sector are detrimental to the 
people of this country. It has to create competition. The concept of privatisation 
is to create competition which should ultimately benefit the consumers. We are 
not here to create monopolies in place of public monopolies. Sir, we seem to 
be enjoying the so-called feel good factor for all our wrong reasons. We have 
got a very huge foreign exchange reserve to the tune of US $ 80 billion, in the 
face of a huge accumulated foreign trade deficit during the last one decade. 
We have a very booming stock market in the face of dwindling industrial 
growth rate and closure of an unprecedented number of industrial units. We 
have been claiming that we have got a very low inflation rate because a large 
section of people, who are employed in agriculture and other rural activities, 
have got very limited money to buy industrial goods. It is not because of the 
fact that the industrial production has gone up. But it is because money that is 
available with the people of this country is very limited and this limited money 
is chasing the goods that are available. That is the reason why, I can analyse, 
there is a low rate of inflation. Inflation, in simple terms, means too much 
money chasing too few goods. We have a situation where there is no money in 
the hands of a larger section of the society to chase even those too few goods. 
Sir, my entire speech is based on one principle. Economic development is the 
panacea of all the evils of this country, both external and internal. If the country 
is developed economically, the country is respected by the comity of nations. 
Internal problems can also be solved and that is the need of the hour. And, the 
Government of India should come forward and the problems that are being 
faced and the concerns that are being expressed to achieve this economic 
growth need to be addressed on a war

good relations with our neighbours. The formulation of the policy should be 
with this focus in mind.
