unwarranted, if the detention is vindictive, if the detention is based on political 
motive... They should review the matter and take necessary steps not only in 
the case of Vaiko but also for all the people in India who have been 
unnecessarily detained in jails. I believe, the Government of India has not 
taken any steps by virtue of section 61 of the Act and has not appointed a 
Review Committee so far. If this Review Committee is appointed, the wishes 
of one crore people of the country, who have signed this memorandum will be 
taken into consideration by the Government of India. So, I request the 
Government of India to take earnest steps to see that the persons who have 
been detained unnecessarily on political grounds or due to political vendetta 
are released from jails. With these words, I conclude.   Thank you. 
SHRI FALI S. NARIMAN (Nominated): Madam Deputy Chairman, I 
thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak. Madam, I congratulate the 
Mover of the Motion of Thanks, my distinguished and hon. friend, Dr. L.M. 
Singhvi for a fine eloquent speech which has set the level of debate. However, 
Madam, permit me to draw attention to a couple of significant points and 
comment on them. They are significant and most relevant points in these 
times to governance in our country. 
289 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February, 2003] 
The first significant point is the complete omission in the President's 
Address about any policy of this Gove rnment with regard to violence and 
perpetrators of violent acts, whoever they be and wheresoever they are seen 
perpetrating them. 
It is true that the President's Address does state that 'we must resolve 
to ensure that communal violence is never repeated in any part of the country.' 
But that is an exhortation to the people of India. There is no signal which only 
the Executive Government at the Centre can give, that all acts of violence by 
whomsoever committed and wheresoever they take place, will be put down 
with a firm hand. 
Madam, messages are frequently conveyed by silence, and the 
silence about this in the President's Address sends the wrong message, such 
as if you have the right political connections, we will look the other way.  This is 
not good for governance in a pluralistic society like ours. 
Secondly, there is no word of solace in the President's Address for 
the victims of violence, whether communal or otherwise - this is very important 
- nor any assurance of early redress. 
The arrogance of religious hatred goes uncontrolled and unpunished 
primarily because those appointed to investigate these events are as yet 
calling no one to account. 
It appears to me that in Gujarat it is not despite the appointment by 
the State Government of a Commission of Inquiry - but because of it, that 
injustice continues to remain the looming casualty of the Godhra and post-
Godhra tragedies. 
In the very first sentence of paragraph 14 of the President's Address 
it is stated that Assembly elections in Gujarat have strengthened democracy.  
Good, they have. 
But then it goes on to say that elections have ended 'a sad chapter in 
the State's history.' Madam, the sad chapter has not ended. It will not end so 
long as no redress is given to the victims of the violence that preceded the 
elections. 
290 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
A clear declaration of Government policy that communal violence 
whether by minority communities or by the majority community will never be 
tolerated, and must never be repeated in any part of the country is, I believe, 
the need of the hour. It is only such a clear declaration that will send the right 
signals to all persons in the country. 
Let me remind the hon. Members of first sentence in paragraph 54. It 
says, "Promotion of social injustice and mainstreaming of the weaker sections 
and the minorities have been the constant endeavour of my Government." 
Mainstreaming of minorities is contrary to the Constitutional mandate. 
Minorities do not require mainstreaming. They require protection, and the 
persons who can protect them and the only authority to whom they can look 
for protection, is the Government of the day. 
I looked closely but did not find anything in the President's Address to 
suggest that the Government of the day has distanced itself from current 
constant threats to minorities whether they be Muslims or Christians, by 
certain sections of the population. It is the Government's duty to gain 
confidence of the minorities and let me hasten to add, it is equally the duty of 
the minorities to do everything in their power and to see that the majority 
community is not, in any way, ridiculed or belittled. 
The President's Address devoted a paragraph to judicial reforms and 
has mentioned that this is envisaged in the Tenth Five Year Plan. Dr. Singhvi 
said that we must give the judicial system a human face. Now, what is the use 
of judicial reforms that don't ensure justice? Where is the human face of 
justice, In a country where an individual is told that he has violated the Official 
Secrets Act by being in possession of a secret document, kept in jail for more 
than six months, and then told that the document was not secret, after all, and 
set free. Any one can commit mistakes. So can the Government. But no one, 
just no one, after the mistake was discovered, has apologised to the individual 
concern - much less to offer him any substantial compensation for what was 
admittedly a wrongful confinement. If he were a citizen of a European country, 
the European Court of Human Rights would have awarded compensation, in a 
handsome sum of hundreds of thousands of Euros. I have been in Delhi now 
for more than thirty years and if there is one trait in the Northen India that I 
have noticed is no one apologises. No one says sorry! But, I did not realise, till 
now, that even the Central Government in Delhi is afflicted with this malignant 
disease. 
291 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February. 2003] 
I welcome the paragraph in the Address that the Ayodhya dispute 
can be resolved, either through negotiations between the two communities or 
through a verdict of the judiciary, which has to be accepted by all concerned. I 
believe it is a statesman-like approach. I would, sincerely, appeal to the hon. 
leaders of the minority community to envisage a possible situation of the 
verdict of the judiciary going against them. Have they ever considered that 
possibility? What will they do then? Prudence points to the path of a 
negotiated settlement. That is the only lasting way to communal peace. There 
is no dearth of eminent religious and social leaders to bring about a solution 
and pride has no place in negotiating an honourable settlement. 
Finally, there is one more important aspect. In the spirited address of 
Dr. Singhvi, on the Motion of Thanks, he has rightly described Parliament as 
not a mere 'talking-shop' or 'debating club' but as 'the national forum of our 
conscience and consensus.'   Very eloquent words. 
I only wish that the Government of the day had lived up to this ideal. 
Parliamentary democracy is a very important, facet of our Constitution. In fact, 
it is the cornerstone of it. But, I regret to say that the reluctance of the 
Government to discuss crucial and controversial matters in the House, and 
taking decision administratively on its own is fast becoming a new feature of 
governance in this country. We, in this House, are, in fact, reduced to a 
'talking-shop' or 'debating club' - and the most expensive one at that. 
I offer, as an example, the disinvestment policy of the Government. I 
have no quarrel* with the disinvestment policy. I personally do not think that 
the Government should engage in business and Article 298 of our 
Constitution, I believe, is only enabling -- carrying on business is not one of the 
essential functions of the Government. Nor do I raise any question about the 
legality of executive action taken on the recently proposed disinvestment. 
When this question was raised in this House, during the last Session, the hon. 
Leader of the Opposition requested the hon. Minister to take the opinion of the 
Attorney General, which he has now taken and has acted on that opinion. And, 
so far as this House is concerned, I believe, the matter must rest there. Since 
we must respect the Office of the Attorney General, as we must respect all the 
Constitutional offices in this country.    But, I am concerned with the propriety 
of action taken on the 
292 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
basis of the opinion of the Attorney General. Legality is not the only facet of 
governance. Propriety is an equal, if not more important, facet. Just as 
corporate democracy requires that even when decisions can lawfully be taken 
by a company's Board of Directors, it is but proper that it should be placed 
before the shareholders of that company for their approval. So also, vital 
national policy decision on disinvestment, even if already taken, should have 
been, as a matter of propriety, placed before the Members of Parliament, 
including the Members of this House, for their approval. It could only then be 
effectively discussed and debated. And, the hon. Minister of Disinvestment is 
amply endowed with powers of persuasion. He could help persuade and 
convince us to accept his proposal. The studied reluctance of the Government 
of the day to bring controversial matters to Parliament is slowly eroding the 
principles of Parliamentary democracy. Bypassing Parliament on vital issue of 
policy is a bad precedent and does not augur well for the future. Madam, 
comparisons with China are odious simply because we do not have the same 
political system as in China. If we were in China, there would have been 
no.debate on disinvestment; there would have been no debate on Ayodhya; 
there would have been no debate on the President's Address. I may not agree 
with what this Government does or does not do. But, I think, we should all 
agree that this system of Government in our Constitution gives us the largest 
measures of freedom. With these few reservations, I have joined the Motion of 
Thanks on the President's Address. 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Madam, I reiterate what my 
colleague Shri Fali S. Nariman has said. When he says that Parliament is the 
supreme body, the supreme forum of national consensus, I agree. The 
President's Address, as we know, is really a Government document. I have 
high respect, regard and affection for the President. But, as we all know, the 
President only reads the Address, which is really a document of the 
Government. This President's Address, perhaps the longest ever, looks more 
like a PIB release with all types of so-called achievements, big or small. But 
behind this, it does hide the fundamentals of the Government's policy, and this 
governance which is divisive, not merely in terms of religion. We all know that 
it is divisive in terms of religion. But in a very insidious way. It is also divisive, 
as far as the social and economic status of people are concerned. It divides 
people in terms of religion, we all know. It also divides the rich and the poor, 
the 'haves' and 'have-nots', the socially high and the socially low.    On the one 
hand, the Government is dividing the 
293 

RAJYA SABHA        [24 February, 2003] 
people of this country, destroying the national unity; on the other hand, it is 
opening wide the doors of this country and its economy, not in great shape, to 
the intents of the profit-making multinational corporations and the 
Governments behind them. This is happening in India. This is happening in 
every country of Asia, Africa and Latin America, at this point of time. What we 
object to, is that this Government is helping and welcoming the efforts at profit 
making by the trans-nationals in everything because people in Developing 
Countries do not really count, even in the spheres of human rights of people, 
fundamental human rights of people, as far as in the case of education or as 
far as health is concerned. Now, this grabbing and profit-making, which looks 
at every thing as only a business and an opportunity for trans-nationals who 
have been allowed entry here and welcomed by the Government. All this is 
being kept under wraps. Therefore, I would just point out here what I have said 
with reference to this very important basic subject which leads to the thought 
process of people, which will decide the future of this country, that is, 
Education. If you look at this book, National Curriculum Framework for School 
Education, which has been produced by the Government itself, you will find a 
clear reference to an educational system that has a dual role. That you will find 
at page 11. It says, "There must be a system of education for those with high 
IQ and emotional quotient." The IQ is a criteria, which had been started in the 
United States, and has been debunked there. The United States wanted to 
give, what we would call in India a non-formal or alternative education, to the 
blacks on the ground that they had inferior IQ. Here, in India, we have added 
'emotional quotient' to the 'intelligence quotient'. The 'emotional quotient', 
which is the creation of this Government, means that those students, who 
have a high spirituality, must be given a special and higher education. Who 
have a high spirituality? Those who don't have to work have a high spirituality. 
The working class cannot afford to have a high spirituality. They are busy 
earning their livelihood. Therefore, that is how, this new curriculum framework 
divides the social elites from the working class. Madam, Deputy Chairman, to 
further elaborate the point, I would like to refer to page 90 of this book. It says 
that whilst those with high Intelligence quotient and emotional quotient will get 
elite education, the rest would get vocational education. And, who are the 
people targeted to get vocational education? They are: the women, the 
Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes and the physically-challenged 
persons. So, all these people, put together, are to be imparted vocational 
training. And those with high spiritual quotient should get elite education.   This 
is how, at the very 
294 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
beginning itself, two classes are being created for children and this is how the 
gap between the elite and the poor masses is being widened. This is how 
divisiveness is being created in the social and economic status of this country. 
We all know, how this Government depends for its survival, for its progress 
on dividing people, on religious lines. This is what is being written in the textbooks 
that follow the national curriculum. To begin with, I shall first refer to this great 
textbook in Social Sciences, named, 'Contemporary India', brought out only a 
couple a months ago, for students of class IX. In this book, there was no 
reference, whatsoever, to the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi by Godse. The 
point had been completely left out. In this textbook, the minorities of our country, 
especially, the Muslims and the Christians, have been defined as anti-nationals, 
and that they played no role in the Freedom Struggle of our country. It is even 
mentioned that the founder of the Aligarh Muslim University was a communal 
element and he was a separatist. This is mentioned in Chapter 3, page 21 
onwards of this book. 
Incidentally, I would like the officials of this Government to please look 
at the edition of this book. This book has two joint editions. One is August, 2002 
edition and the other is September, 2002 edition. On both these books it is 
mentioned, 'first edition'. How can a book have two first editions? This is 
something which I am unable to understand. There is another an August, 2002 
edition, which I am now referring to. Then, there is September, 2002 edition, 
on which it is mentioned that it is the first reprint of October. All this is very 
confusing. The officials in the department must inquire into this. They also look at 
the number of print orders given. For the first edition of September, 2002, a print 
order of 3,75,000 has been given and for the August, 2002, edition 2,25,000 
print orders were placed. That makes a total of 6,00,000 copies. For whom so 
many copies have been printed? In the previous years, never have so many 
copies been printed for Class IX Social Sciences students. It has never gone 
beyond 2.5 lakhs. Why were so many English copies published this year? The 
number of English and Hindi copies taken together would be more. But, for the 
present, let us keep the number of Hindi copies aside. Why were so many English 
copies published? The matter is questionable because the main user of this 
book, the Delhi Government, and many private schools, had refused to use 
that book. There is hanky-panky in this. There is something fishy in this.  The 
Department should look into this. 
295 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
The point which however I would like to highlight here is the way 
this textbook communalises the situation. While communalising, it also 
gives wrong facts, historically. For instance, it is mentioned that Goa, 
Daman and Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli were, collectively, called Goa. It is 
like saying, during the British Rule, India was called Delhi because the 
Government was based in Delhi. This is the type of historical and factual 
inaccuracies given in this book. Not only that... (Interruptions)... they also 
glorify things. In this book, there is a reference to communal Muslim and 
Christian organisations and their anti-national activities. But, as far as other 
communities are concerned there were no communal elements. On page 
61, it is mentioned that Dadra and Nagar Haveli was captured by the Jan 
Sangh. This is totally against history. The Chief Minister of the then 
Bombay State, went on to become the Prime Minister, Shri Morarji Desai. In 
Volume II of "The Story of my Life", written by Shri Morarji Desai, at pages 
47-49, it has been written, how he had directed the Reserve Police to 
encircle Dadra and Nagar Haveli, so that Portuguese troops did not come. 
Then, it has been written, when the Portuguese police officers which were 
four or five in number, saw the Reserve Police which looked like a military 
force, they did not attack and ran away into the adjacent forests. There 
was no fight whatsoever. No fighting took place. That is what Mr. Morarji Desai 
said. Why do you want to glorify Jan Sangh on wrong facts? I am sure that Jan 
Sangh has done some good, but not this. This is what the historians should 
really advert to. There are people who know the facts. There are people who 
were part of this process and were fully aware of it. (Time bell rings) Madam, 
please give me five minutes to make some important points. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Mr. Faleiro, a lot of time has been taken.   
We have to accommodate all the speakers. 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: Madam, that is true. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: You are taking the time of your Party 
speakers. 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: Madam, I just want to say that this 
Government is trying to divide the country on social, economic and religious 
basis. On the other hand, it is welcoming all the trans-national corporations 
which are trying to gobble up our educational system.   Until 2002) in fact, 
296 

[24 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
until 14 th January, 2002, the position was that, at school level, no student 
could have foreign schooling unless he was a son or daughter of a diplomat or 
a foreigner, or her or she who had intended to pursue a course which was not 
available in India. Now, after 14 th January, 2002, anybody, whosoever it may 
be, can take up here at school level itself, any course abroad. All the big talk 
of the hon. Minister about Indianisation, spiritualisation and nationalism is 
meaningless. Now, for a student, who wants to do any course from Britain, or 
France or America, nobody's permission is required to be taken. That thing 
has been waived. Therefore, again, we are going to create, in this country, two 
classes of people. One, who have their education from foreign countries, even 
at the school level here and the others who have their education - third rate 
education - at the schools, the Government is providing in the name of 
informal education. The more we abuse Pakistan, the more we are following 
their system, because this system is prevailing there. There also the elite 
people have their education in the Western model and the rest have their 
education in Madrases. Even in my own State, Government has clcsed 
Primary Schools and handed them over to Vidya Bharati. This is being done at 
a time when Pakistan and Afghanistan, which have their educational system 
on fundamentalist group basis, are trying to become more liberal. This is what 
appears to be happening. We are, tragically, following the reverse mood, that 
is, moving from secularism to communalism, while it appears from the reports, 
that in Afghanistan and Pakistan people are trying to move, to some extent, 
however limited it might be, from a fundamentalist type of education to a 
liberal education. {Time bell rings) I just want to say this and conclude ; At this 
point of time the Ministry of Human Resource Development and the Ministry of 
Commerce are busy preparing proposals for opening our education system to 
foreign business concerns. The Government should inform this House what 
they intend to do next month at GATS. It should take the consensus of this 
House, because GATS is an irreversible process. It cannot be reversed by 
future Governments. GATS process is not subject to Indian courts.   It is 
subjected to their own courts. 
AN HON. MEMBER: Are you referring to GATS or WTO? 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO: I am referring to GATS. I have found 
one Vice-Chancellor who does not know what GATS is all about. This is 
because of secrecy. And you should not be surprised if we don't know what 
GATS is. GATS is a General Agreement on Trade in services which is part or 
a branch, a follow-up of WTO. The Government must discuss this 
297 

RAJYA SABHA [24 February, 2003] 
issue in this House. It should inform the House what it intends to do next 
month in terms of commitments and opportunities available under GATT in the 
field of education and health. The Government must withdraw the book 
"National Curriculum Framework for School Education" which is divisive and 
destroys the unity of the country for now and for the generations to come.
